question: In 2023, the company Nueva Pescanova announced the opening of the world’s first industrial octopus farm in the Canary Islands, aiming for an annual production of 3 000 tonnes – equivalent to one million octopuses. Beside the immense suffering inflicted on these sentient beings, it is essential to highlight the ecological impact of such intensive production.

The production of feed on these farms requires millions of tonnes of fish and consumes vast quantities of water, which intensifies the already critical water stress and overfishing in the region. Compassion in World Farming reported that the European Maritime, Fisheries, and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) provided nearly 40 % of the funding for the Nueva Pescanova octopus farming project, which amounts to EUR 3.6 million.
Does the Commission plan to make the EMFAF more conditional on strict animal welfare and environmental criteria?
How does the Commission intend to strengthen control and transparency of the EMFAF, in order to guarantee that only sustainable aquaculture practices are cofinanced?

Given that establishing octopus farms conflicts with EU goals to align animal welfare legislation with the latest scientific evidence, end overfishing and reduce the environmental impact of our food system: does the Commission confirm that octopus farms cause significant harm and how far has it progressed with measures to prevent the production and importation of industrially farmed octopuses?
answer: 1. Under the Commission proposal for the EU budget 2028-2034, a new single Fund will finance the Member States’ National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRP Plans), covering different policy areas, including fisheries and aquaculture. In the future, there is a clear shift in the delivery model of the funding. Payments will be made conditional on the achievement of milestones and targets.

The legal framework will no longer include detailed eligibility rules. Instead, it will be up to the Member States and regions to implement measures according to their needs and priorities. This should help maximise support for the sector across different funds. 2.
The proposal for the new budget includes the principle of ‘do-no-significant-harm’ (DNSH) which will apply to the entire EU budget, in line with the EU Financial Regulation (1).

This principle mandates that all programmes and activities must fulfil their intended goals and set objectives according to sector-specific guidelines, ensuring they do not fund any activities that could cause considerable harm and hinder environmental objectives. 3.

The EU strategic aquaculture guidelines (2) recommend that the Commission and Member States support diversification of EU aquaculture to types of aquacultures with better environmental performance and promote the use of sustainably sourced feed ingredients for fed aquaculture. The EU Reference Centre for the welfare of aquatic animals plays an important role to fulfil gaps in scientific knowledge.
